question: Recent news reports suggest that major AI companies are buying, scanning and then destroying large quantities of antique and modern books to train their AI systems, thus destroying cultural heritage to train their AI models. An internal paper from Anthropic even explicitly states the objective of ‘destructively scanning all the books in the world’.

The main purpose of this ‘destructive scanning’ of books appears to be to circumvent copyright issues, as it may be covered by the fair use provisions of US copyright law. However, there are also reports that EU booksellers have been approached to supply books for this purpose, with the books being shipped and destroyed overseas. Can the Commission: 1.

Outline which measures it is considering to prevent the potential circumvention of EU copyright law and the destruction of EU cultural heritage through the international shipping of books from the EU to non-EU countries for the purpose of ‘destructive scanning’?
Confirm whether it will address this issue in its forthcoming initiative on AI and copyright?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) As the Commission noted in its reply to written question E-002819/2026, the scanning and/or digitisation of books protected by copyright constitutes an act of reproduction requiring the rightsholder’s consent unless a relevant exception applies.

The exceptions for text and data mining1 apply to text and data in digital form and do not cover scanning and/or digitisation of physical works. Where no exception applies, the digitisation of books without authorisation is an infringement of EU copyright law. Rightsholders can enforce their rights before courts and make use of the remedies provided for under, inter alia, Directive 2004/48/EC2.

The destruction of the books in question remains a matter of national law, in particular of legislation on moral rights3. The Commission has the power to ensure that Member States comply with their obligations under EU copyright law.

In addition, the AI Act4 requires providers placing general-purpose AI models on the EU market to put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law and to disclose sufficiently detailed summaries of training data. These obligations extend to all protected content, including physical books used for AI training. The Commission started enforcing these rules in August 2026.

The Commission is exploring the need for additional measures under EU copyright law to help rightsholders enforce their rights in the age of AI, while supporting AI innovation. Following a call for evidence5, the Commission launched a targeted consultation to gather feedback on challenges and possible policy options6.
The Commission is also preparing an AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors to promote an approach to AI that reinforces human creativity, cultural diversity, and respects creators’ rights.
1 Articles 3 and 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on

copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/48/oj/eng. 3 Recital 19 of Directive 2001/29/EC. 4 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng. 5 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.
